title.narrative: Strengthening Women’s Ability for the Productive New Opportunities (SWAPNO-II)
Strengthening Women’s Ability for the Productive New Opportunities (SWAPNO-II)

description.narrative:
The extended phase of SWAPNO II proposes utilising different livelihood skill development training, life skill training, engagement with additional income-generating activities and access to different service providing agencies which will lead to the ultimate goal of the project: "Increased productivity as well as profitability, productive employment, and ensured social, economic, and environmental benefits". This will be delivered through three inter-linked outcomes of the project,
Outcome (i): Increased income and assets engaging local economy and skill development,
Outcome (ii): Strengthened human capabilities to build climate resilience capacity, and
Outcome (iii) Strengthen institutional capacity for sustaining SWAPNO benefits.
During the proposed extended phase, SWAPNO II will support another 10,044 underprivileged and climate vulnerable rural women from 10 poorest districts of Northern flood prone areas and Southern Coastal zone of Bangladesh. In addition, the project will provide need-based follow-up support to 3,564 women from the current phase who already graduated from extreme poverty.

Detta projekt syftar till att lyfta några av Bangladeshs fattigaste kvinnor, som lever på landsbygden i delar av landet som är särskilt utsatta för klimatförändringarnas negativa effekter, ut ur extrem fattigdom genom att dra nytta av produktiva inkomstmöjligheter. Den primära målgruppen är 3600 kvinnor i Kurigram, Lalmonirhat, Gaibandha och Jamalpur distrikten även om betydligt fler människor, inklusive dessa kvinnors barn, kommer att dra viss nytta av projektets positiva effekter.
SWAPNO-II syftar till att öka målgruppens inkomster och tillgångar genom att vidga deras valmöjligheter, öka deras kapacitet att göra val, stärka deras motståndskraft mot externa chocker, inklusive klimatrelaterade katastrofer och öka deras tillgång till finansiella tjänster samt se till att projektets fördelar kvarstår över tid.
Målen ska nås genom en kombination av ansträngningar. Kvinnorna anställs först i offentliga arbeten fora att återuppbygga eller klimatsäkra kritisk infrastruktur och för det arbetet får det en liten, men säker lön var fjortonde dag under ett halvår. En del av lönen sparas automatiskt och den delen får kvinnorna tillgång till som en större engångssumma vid anställningsperiodens slut. Meningen är att den ska möjliggöra för kvinnorna att starta sina egna småföretag. Kvinnorna får också utbildning i olika vardagskunskaper och lite yrkeskunskaper som är relevanta för att hitta anställning eller starta eget företag vilket ökar deras nätverk och personliga värdighet. Stöd ges också för tillgång till digitala finansiella tjänster och försäkringar. Idén är att kvinnornas ökade inkomster, kombinerat med ökade kunskaper och självsäkerhet ska hjälpa dem att investera på ett produktivt sätt som ger dem avkastning under kommande år. Dessutom bidar projektet till att öka de lokala myndigheternas kapacitet att implementera fattigdomsreducerande och genderkänsliga sociala transfereringssystem.

This project aims at sustainably lifting some of Bangladesh’s poorest women, living in rural areas prone to the negative effects of climate change, of out of extreme poverty, primarily by making use of productive income-generating opportunities. The main beneficiaries are 3600 women in the districts of Kurigram, Lalmonirhat, Gaibandha and Jamalpur even if a substantially larger number of people, including these women’s children, will benefit, to various extents, from the positive effects of this project.
SWAPNO-II aims to increase the targeted women’s income and assets by expanding their choices, enhance their capabilities for exercising choices, strengthen their resilience to shocks, including disasters and climate change, and enhance their financial inclusion and ensure that the benefits are sustainable over time.
This will be achieved through a combination of efforts. The women will first be engaged in public-works to rehabilitate and/or climate proof critical local infrastructure for which they receive a small, predictable, fortnightly, salary during a period of six months. A part of the remuneration is set aside in compulsory savings which the women will access as a lump-sum at the end of the public-works period to allow them to, for example start their own small-scale businesses. They will also be trained in various life-skills as well as skills relevant for future employments, enhancing their networks and contributing to personal dignity. Assistance will also be provided to access digital financial services and insurance schemes. The idea is that their increased income combined with life and employability skills and enhance self-esteem will help beneficiaries invest productively to ensure a stream of income in years to come. Moreover, the capacity of the local government to implement pro-poor, gender-sensitive social-transfer projects will be enhanced.

title.narrative: Sustainable Graduation from Exxtreme Poverty of SWAPNO Women Project-II

description.narrative:
This conclusion on performance is prepared based on the Annual Report 2025, covering the period from 1 January to 31 December 2025, field visits conducted by the responsible programme officer and controller at the Embassy of Sweden during 2025, and several meetings with the UNDP SWAPNO II team.
The project reported substantial progress in beneficiaries economic resilience. Average monthly household income increased from BDT 4,618 at baseline to BDT 7,558, representing a 64% increase. The proportion of households above the Lower Poverty Line rose from 10.4% to 47.8%, while 84% of households purchased assets, mainly livestock, poultry and business equipment. The share of households without savings fell from 88.9% to 4%. Through ROSCA groups, beneficiaries mobilised approximately BDT 5.7 crore and invested in 16,794 income-generating activities. These results indicate increased capacity to save, invest, diversify livelihoods and manage economic risks.
Womens economic agency also strengthened. Around 99% of beneficiaries reported control over income, savings and household assets, compared with 65% at baseline. Women increasingly participate in decisions on purchasing and selling assets and independently use bank or mobile financial service accounts. Food security improved, with 98% of surveyed households consuming three meals per day, while self-reported health status improved for 84% of beneficiaries. These results suggest changes in household decision-making, financial behaviour, food consumption and use of formal health services.
At the institutional and community levels, Union Parishads and Union Disaster Management Committees strengthened their knowledge and practices concerning gender-responsive disaster management, climate adaptation and pro-poor service delivery. Forty-five per cent of surveyed beneficiaries reported applying climate-adaptive livelihood practices, and 44% participated in community disaster-related activities. Beneficiaries increasingly contributed to early warning, infrastructure maintenance, environmental protection and post-disaster recovery, demonstrating a shift from being recipients of support to active community participants.
Expected results
The expected results of increased income, consumption, savings, productive assets, food security and womens economic decision-making were largely achieved. Public works employment provided immediate income while livelihood activities, ROSCA savings and productive investments supported a gradual transition towards more diversified sources of income. Most beneficiaries reported combining project-supported wage income with other livelihood activities, suggesting reduced dependence on temporary wage employment alone. The movement of households into higher income and expenditure categories and above national poverty thresholds supports the central project logic of progressing from short-term employment towards greater economic stability and poverty graduation.
Expected improvements in womens empowerment were also reported. Women gained greater control over income, savings, assets and financial accounts, while their participation in household economic decisions increased. Some women also entered occupations traditionally considered unsuitable for women, including shoe production and repair, while others moved into formal employment in the garment sector. These examples indicate changes in womens confidence, family roles and community perceptions regarding the types of work women are capable of performing.
The project also achieved expected institutional results by strengthening relationships between beneficiaries, Union Parishads, UDMCs and government technical departments such as the Department of Agricultural Extension and the Department of Livestock. Local institutions reportedly adopted more participatory and gender-responsive approaches to disaster preparedness and service delivery. Beneficiary groups were linked with government services, markets, financial institutions, health providers and protection mechanisms, while Union-level apex bodies and youth-led structures were proposed to maintain these relationships after project closure.
Unexpected results
Several results exceeded planned targets. Women-led enterprises reached 314 against a target of 100, apprenticeship training reached 1,200 against 622, and public assets supporting disaster and climate-risk reduction reached 5,344 against 1,132. ROSCA savings also created a notable leverage effect by financing a large number of beneficiary-owned livelihood activities.
However, some important results were below expectations. Viable household micro-businesses reached 996 against a target of 4,000, formal-sector employment reached 632 against 2,000, and local employment generated through enterprises reached 236 against 622. Household responsibilities, caregiving burdens, reluctance to relocate and limited formal-sector absorption reduced participation. In response, UNDP realigned resources towards home-based livelihoods and apprenticeship opportunities and introduced childcare support at training centres. This demonstrates adaptive management based on implementation experience and beneficiary constraints.
Conclusion:
Overall, the project achieved credible and important household-level results in income, savings, productive investment, food security, health access and womens economic agency. Beneficiaries appear better able to manage financial resources, invest in livelihoods, access services and participate in household and community decision-making. Local institutions also strengthened their coordination with beneficiary groups and their gender-responsive and climate-related practices.
The projects theory of change remains broadly valid. However, the formal-employment and enterprise-led employment pathways have performed below the originally expected scale. The sustainability of income, enterprises, ROSCA groups, government service linkages and local institutional arrangements should therefore be closely assessed through the exit strategy, endline evaluation and post-project follow-up.
